---
title: "Bias-Variance Tradeoff"
description: "The balance between systematic model error and sensitivity to training data."
term: "Bias-Variance Tradeoff"
letter: "B"
category: "Machine Learning"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

The bias-variance tradeoff describes two ways a model can fail to
generalize. A model with too much bias may be too simple to capture useful
patterns; a model with too much variance may fit its training data too
closely and change substantially with new samples.

## Technical explanation

Under common assumptions for squared-error regression, expected prediction
error can be decomposed into squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise:

$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(y-\hat{f}(x))^2\right]
= \operatorname{Bias}[\hat{f}(x)]^2
+ \operatorname{Var}[\hat{f}(x)]
+ \sigma^2
$$

This decomposition is illustrative and does not apply unchanged to every
loss function or learning setting.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

The concept helps interpret underfitting and overfitting and guides
decisions about model capacity, regularization, and data collection.
Practical evaluation on held-out data remains necessary; the tradeoff is
not a direct tuning formula.

## How it works

Increasing model flexibility can reduce systematic error but may make the
fitted model more sensitive to the particular training sample. More data,
regularization, and suitable model selection can change this balance.
Validation performance helps estimate how well a chosen model generalizes.

## Practical example

A straight-line model may underfit a strongly curved relationship, showing
high bias. A very high-degree polynomial can fit training noise and perform
poorly on new points, showing high variance.

## Common misconceptions

- The tradeoff is not a rule that every reduction in bias must increase
  variance by a fixed amount.
- Training error alone cannot reveal generalization performance.
- The decomposition depends on assumptions and should not be treated as an
  exact account of every modern model's behaviour.
